item.title: Report: Research Gold offers '100% human-written, never AI' medical research but uses AI-generated reviewers and unauthorized identities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Research Gold, a company claiming to provide fully human-written medical research services, including peer-reviewed manuscripts and systematic reviews, is using AI-generated profiles for its listed PhD reviewers and methodologists. Some real methodologists' identities and photos were used without their consent, and the company's communications, including phone and email interactions, are AI-driven despite claims of human expertise. The company advertises adherence to established research standards like PRISMA 2020 and the Cochrane Handbook, but investigations found that key team members do not exist and have no online presence or publication history. After being contacted, Research Gold removed the unauthorized real individuals from its website. Attempts to verify the company's claimed contributions to published papers have not received responses from lead authors. This revelation raises concerns about transparency and authenticity in outsourced medical research services, highlighting risks for researchers relying on such companies for critical academic work.

item.title: Google explains why Go is well-suited for AI-assisted software engineering, emphasizing its platform approach and tooling for code review and maintenance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google highlights that Go's design focuses on software engineering principles that support collaboration, maintainability, and long-term system evolution, which align well with AI-assisted coding workflows. The language's integrated toolchain, including formatting, testing, dependency management, and security features, helps both human developers and AI agents produce higher-quality, more reliable code. Go's uniform ecosystem and standard library promote consistency across projects, enabling AI models to operate more efficiently and accurately on Go code. This structural coherence benefits teams managing large codebases and supports the evolving role of AI as a coding collaborator rather than a sole code writer.

item.title: Researchers decode hidden reasoning traces from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google LLM APIs, revealing thousands of leaked sensitive artifacts including API keys and passwords [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrated that proprietary large language model APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google leak encrypted reasoning traces that can be decoded to reveal hidden tokens. By analyzing over 6,700 publicly available agent trajectories, they reconstructed more than 315,000 reasoning blocks containing sensitive information such as API keys, passwords, access tokens, and personal data. The study found 704 distinct privacy artifacts, with 64 appearing exclusively in the hidden reasoning blocks and not in visible session data. This raises concerns about the confidentiality of user data processed by these models and highlights the need for improved security measures to prevent unintended information exposure.

item.title: X.ai launches Grok Bot to automate tasks across user apps and websites, including complex tools like Zendesk [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: X.ai has introduced Grok Bot, an AI assistant designed to operate within users' existing applications and websites by mimicking their interactions. The bot can log in once and perform tasks across multiple platforms, including navigating complex tools such as Zendesk to manage support queues efficiently.

item.title: OpenAI's head of ethics departs less than a year after joining the company
item.description: OpenAI's head of ethics has left the company less than a year after joining, marking a significant leadership change in the organization's approach to ethical oversight. The departure highlights ongoing challenges in managing ethics within rapidly evolving AI companies.

item.title: Researchers find chain-of-thought prompting improves large language model reasoning on high-depth tasks but is redundant or harmful on shallow or intermediate tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study investigates the impact of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on large language model (LLM) reasoning, revealing that CoT helps overcome an architectural bottleneck related to serial computation exceeding a transformer's single-pass capacity. The research evaluates three instruction-tuned models across five NLP benchmarks, showing significant accuracy gains on complex, high-depth tasks like GSM8K and MATH, but minimal or negative effects on simpler tasks such as MMLU and ARC. The findings suggest CoT acts as a bandwidth bypass that aids tasks requiring extensive serial computation but offers little benefit for tasks that fit within the model's single-pass capacity.

item.title: Researchers identify procedural fairness failures in RLHF due to preference averaging, propose Preference-Aware RLHF to improve alignment accuracy and reduce fairness gaps [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new study finds that Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) often aggregates diverse human preferences into a single reward model, assuming homogeneity and causing majority preferences to dominate while minority views are under-represented. This leads to procedural fairness failures in alignment, where distinct preference signals are lost during reward modeling. The researchers introduce Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF), which separates optimization across different preference modes during reward learning, improving overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reducing fairness gaps between groups. The work demonstrates that structural design choices in reward learning can cause fairness issues even in controlled, noise-free environments. These findings have direct implications for large language models and agentic systems, where biased reward models may exacerbate inequities across sequential decisions, highlighting the need for more nuanced approaches to preference aggregation in AI alignment.

item.title: Riemann GeoResolver introduces a non-Euclidean attention framework extending inverse-distance attention from Euclidean to hyperbolic and spherical geometries with theoretical guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper presents the Riemann GeoResolver, a theoretical framework that generalizes inverse-distance attention from a Euclidean prototype to non-Euclidean settings using hyperbolic and spherical geometries. The authors prove three core theorems for the Euclidean case, demonstrating improved retrieval efficiency, convergence properties, and noise memorization limits compared to softmax attention. The framework then extends these results by replacing Euclidean distances with hyperbolic geodesic distances for memory storage and spherical geodesic distances for routing, integrating ten modules including curvature compression, gradient bounds, and sparse routing. The work establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation connecting Euclidean attention as a special case to more general hyperbolic memory and spherical retrieval mechanisms. The Euclidean theorems are fully proved, while analogous arguments support the non-Euclidean extensions, offering new insights into attention mechanisms across different geometric spaces.

item.title: Researchers propose cost-aware cross-tier transfer method for evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts, reducing search costs by up to 54x while maintaining performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present a method to optimize large language model (LLM) prompts and agentic programs by decoupling LLM roles and running high-volume answering on cheaper tiers, reserving stronger models for rare reflection and variation steps. This approach enables upward cross-tier transfer, deploying cheaply evolved prompts on stronger target models, significantly lowering search costs. The study evaluates this method across four tasks and eleven models from four families, showing that it matches or exceeds same-tier optimization while using over 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier. Cost reductions range from 5.6 to 14 times, increasing to 25 to 54 times when reasoning tiers generate long chains of thought during fitness evaluations.

item.title: Researchers introduce Behavioral Mode Axes to control large language model behavioral styles using 3,200 scenarios across 20 patterns and four prompt registers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a situated behavioral-data framework to study and control large language model (LLM) behavioral personalities, using 3,200 contrastive scenarios covering 20 behavioral patterns and four prompt registers based on validated psychometric facets. They find that LLMs exhibit stable, model-specific behavioral profiles with register-dependent shifts in decisions, advice-giving, and task execution. The study introduces Behavioral Mode Axes (BMAs), activation-space directions derived from behavioral traces, to control these patterns more effectively, with thought-derived BMAs providing cleaner control than response-derived ones. This approach suggests LLM personality-like tendencies are better understood as measurable and controllable behavioral modes grounded in interaction contexts rather than abstract self-report traits.

item.title: Researchers introduce ConVAWG, a retrieval-grounded framework generating controlled synthetic multi-turn dialogues modeling Violence Against Women and Girls scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed ConVAWG, a framework designed to generate synthetic multi-turn dialogues that model conversational dynamics in Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios. The system builds scenarios using persona seeds, demographic data from the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and Domestic Homicide Review cases, converting these into hierarchical event timelines and role-play dialogues with targeted toxicity control. ConVAWG addresses challenges in accessing and annotating real conversation data in sensitive domains by releasing over 6,000 dialogue events across 200 scenarios with detailed metadata. Evaluations including human assessments and large language model judgments demonstrate strong dialogue quality and fidelity to the domain, supporting research into relational and temporally unfolding abuse phenomena beyond sentence-level toxicity.

item.title: AXIOM launches a trust-first neuro-symbolic system for natural-language mathematical reasoning with 90% accuracy and self-explaining step traces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AXIOM is a neuro-symbolic architecture that converts informal math problems into a structured schema processed by a deterministic computer algebra system (CAS) to derive and verify answers or abstain. It uses a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompts, and CAS handlers, with 4,783 routes deployed, 71% answering without invoking the language model, and no regressions in correctness. On the MATH test set, AXIOM achieves 90.2% accuracy with one confident wrong answer, and on held-out MATH-500 data, it scores 89.2% with zero confident wrong answers, demonstrating robustness beyond memorization. The system also answers a 20,000-record arithmetic benchmark at 100% accuracy in 1 ms per record and has served approximately 30,000 public queries. AXIOM emphasizes trustworthiness by treating abstentions as first-class outputs and enabling continuous improvement without regressions, applying disciplined methods like math-template bucketing and regression scanning. This approach aims to extend trustworthy neuro-symbolic reasoning beyond mathematics.

item.title: Researchers train probes on LLM pre-generation activations to predict success on math and coding tasks, enabling up to 70% inference cost reduction by routing queries across models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated whether large language models (LLMs) encode their likelihood of success in internal representations before generating outputs, aiming to improve inference efficiency. They trained linear probes on pre-generation activations to predict task-specific success, outperforming surface features like question length, and demonstrated that models encode a notion of difficulty distinct from human difficulty, especially with extended reasoning. Using the E2H-AMC dataset, which includes both human and model performance on identical problems, the team showed that leveraging these probes to route queries across multiple models can surpass the best single model's performance while reducing inference costs by up to 70% on math tasks. This approach highlights how internal model representations can guide more efficient computation even when they diverge from human intuitions about problem difficulty.

item.title: Researchers study recurrent-depth transformers for implicit reasoning, showing improved compositional generalization and depth extrapolation over vanilla transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate implicit reasoning in transformer models, focusing on the ability to combine knowledge or rules within a single forward pass. They study recurrent-depth transformers, which perform iterative computation over the same layers, to address limitations in compositional generalization and multi-hop reasoning depth. Their controlled experiments demonstrate that recurrent-depth transformers outperform vanilla transformers in systematic generalization and depth extrapolation tasks, with generalization emerging through a three-stage grokking process and improved reasoning depth enabled by scaling inference-time recurrence. The study also explores how training strategies influence depth extrapolation and identifies a key limitation called overthinking, where excessive recurrence during inference degrades prediction quality and restricts generalization to very deep reasoning tasks. These findings provide guidance for training recurrent-depth transformers and highlight their potential for enhanced implicit reasoning capabilities in language models.

item.title: Researchers propose L2C framework for causal discovery with latent variables, learning cluster structure from local causal patterns without manual mapping [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The L2C (Local to Cluster Causal Abstraction) framework addresses challenges in causal discovery posed by latent variables and unknown cluster assignments. It learns cluster structures from local causal patterns and represents each cluster with up to three micro-variables, enabling macro-level causal reasoning without prior cluster knowledge. The method uses local discovery on maximal ancestral graphs to identify direct causes, effects, and V-structures, followed by cluster-level inference through a specialized calculus. L2C is sound, complete, and computationally efficient, connecting micro-level information to macro causal effects in complex settings where latent variables are unavoidable.

item.title: Researchers propose stage-wise preference optimization with hard examples to reduce hallucination in multimodal large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers address hallucination in vision-language models, where generated responses may be linguistically plausible but visually inconsistent, by introducing a stage-wise preference optimization framework that constructs targeted multimodal data near known failure boundaries. Their approach focuses on ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training to improve grounding consistency and reduce hallucination. Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world scenarios demonstrate that this method produces more visually grounded and informative responses compared to several leading proprietary models. The findings suggest hallucination arises not only from limited model capacity but also from autoregressive generation's tendency to favor plausible linguistic continuations under weak visual grounding, indicating future research directions in physical consistency modeling and uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning.

item.title: Researchers introduce a Multi-Group Item Response Theory model to analyze safety degradation in large language models across 10 languages, revealing language-specific vulnerabilities and mistranslation impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a Multi-Group Item Response Theory (IRT) framework to disentangle factors affecting safety degradation in large language models across multiple languages. Evaluating 61 model configurations on 1.9 million responses from 10 languages, they found that safety failures are primarily driven by a shared mechanism but vary by language and prompt type, with some models more vulnerable in English than in low-resource languages. The study highlights that mistranslations and cultural mismatches contribute to safety gaps, especially in physical harm categories like theft and weapons. The IRT framework outperforms traditional metrics by accurately predicting safety vulnerabilities even when entire languages are excluded from training data. This approach enables fairer cross-lingual safety evaluation and suggests targeted improvements in dataset construction to address concept-language mismatches and reduce safety risks in multilingual AI systems.

item.title: Researchers find context-truthfulness is preserved across large language model lineages and propose TruthProbe to enhance truthful attention heads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated whether foundational large language models (LLMs) and their specialized multimodal variants (MLLMs) share behavioral traits related to context-truthfulness. They quantified truthfulness at the attention-head level across diverse model families including Vicuna, Qwen2.5, LLaMA2, and Mistral, finding that truth scores are strongly preserved within lineages even after instruction tuning or multimodal adaptation. This preservation aligns with attention-head weight retention, with truthful heads focusing on query-relevant evidence. Building on these findings, the team introduced TruthProbe, a soft-gating method that amplifies context-truthful heads while maintaining other head contributions. TruthProbe improved contextual truthfulness on benchmarks like HaluEval and reduced multimodal hallucinations on POPE and CHAIR datasets. The approach leverages the inheritance of truthfulness from base LLMs to their fine-tuned descendants, and the researchers have made their code publicly available.

item.title: Researchers identify and correct structural-role bias in KV cache eviction for long-context LLMs, improving accuracy on schema-dense inputs like nested JSON [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed attention-based KV cache eviction methods used in long-context language models and found that these methods disproportionately retain non-content tokens such as delimiters and structural keys, which degrade exact-match accuracy significantly under tight memory budgets. They demonstrated that suppressing structural key tokens during cache eviction improves signal-to-noise ratio and accuracy, especially at low memory budgets. The team introduced a retraining-free, role-conditional allocation method over existing scoring mechanisms, which recovers most of the accuracy loss without additional training and incurs negligible inference cost using a small linear role probe. While this approach closes much of the performance gap, matching parser-level downstream accuracy remains an open challenge.

item.title: Researchers analyze converting large pretrained transformers to smaller models, finding representation alignment but weak parameter alignment and proposing initialization-based conversion methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied the conversion of a 1.4 billion parameter transformer model to a smaller 410 million parameter sibling within the Pythia family, finding strong alignment in representations but weak alignment in parameters. They showed that dense weight projection disrupts key model structures and that the value of conversion lies primarily in initialization rather than direct weight transfer. The team decomposed conversion into two independent methods: least-squares compensation, which improves zero-shot performance efficiently, and variance-preserving rescaling, which benefits endpoint performance after continued pre-training.

item.title: Researchers find reasoning language models fail to strategically allocate shared test-time compute across questions with varying difficulty and value [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce an exam-style evaluation framework to study how reasoning language models distribute a shared token budget across questions of different difficulty and point values. They find that current models tend to allocate compute greedily by question order, front-loading effort on early questions and ignoring question value, a pattern that worsens as the number of questions increases. Explicit planning prompts help spread compute more evenly but do not lead to value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. This behavior is consistent across mathematical and code reasoning tasks, highlighting a distinct challenge in global budget allocation not captured by conventional per-question evaluations.

item.title: Researchers introduce Imaginative Generative AI framework to enhance diversity in generative models beyond data distribution limits using spectral entropy constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Imaginative Generative AI (IGA), a framework that incorporates diversity as a design objective for generative models by selecting distributions with prescribed spectral diversity levels relative to a reference. IGA measures diversity using von Neumann entropy of the kernel covariance operator in a fixed representation space, defining an Entropy Wall that separates regimes of diversity repair within data limits and imaginative generation beyond them. The framework develops an entropy-constrained projection theory and introduces IGA Guidance, a retraining-free inference method compatible with score-based and diffusion models like DDPM and DDIM. Experiments on synthetic and vision benchmarks demonstrate IGA's ability to recover lost diversity below the Entropy Wall and to extrapolate spectral diversity beyond it, enabling controlled generation that extends beyond mere imitation of training data.

item.title: Researchers introduce ELBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark evaluating education-focused large language models on capability, safety, instructional usefulness, and pedagogical alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed ELBench, the first benchmark designed to assess large language models used in education across four integrated dimensions: general capability, safety and trustworthiness, basic education, and high-level cultivation. The benchmark combines curated public datasets with newly created safety and cultivation data to evaluate models under a common protocol. Nine models were tested, including seven general-purpose and two education-specialized systems, revealing that module-level evaluations provide more insight than aggregate scores and that safety often inversely correlates with practical teaching effectiveness. The study found that Chinese-developed models lead in safety, particularly on region-specific normative content, while education-specialized models did not outperform others in education modules. Additionally, all models showed a shared limitation in high-level cultivation tasks, favoring pedagogical style over alignment with stated goals. These findings highlight challenges in aligning domain-specific training with frontier system performance on educational tasks and suggest areas for future improvement in education-facing AI models.

item.title: Researchers introduce SPOT, a sampling-based framework for interpreting deep reinforcement learning policies with finite-horizon trees and formal accuracy guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SPOT (Sampling Policy Observation Tree), a model-agnostic framework that interprets deep reinforcement learning (DRL) policies by constructing finite-horizon trees through action sampling and state simulation. This approach provides an empirical view of policy action preferences and potential future outcomes, with formal guarantees on accuracy. The method was demonstrated in traffic-signal control scenarios, allowing detailed inspection of policy behaviors beyond traditional single-step analysis.

item.title: Researchers propose MIDAS framework for incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis using mutual information disentanglement and uncertainty-aware fusion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed MIDAS, a new framework designed to improve multimodal sentiment analysis when some data modalities are incomplete or corrupted. MIDAS uses a variational approach to represent each modality with Gaussian latent variables, separating shared and exclusive information, and employs a minimax objective to disentangle these factors while enhancing semantic alignment. It also introduces an uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism that weights features based on their reliability to ensure robust integration despite incomplete data. The framework was tested on three widely used datasets and demonstrated consistent performance gains over existing methods across various incomplete data scenarios. MIDAS addresses limitations of prior approaches that relied on data imputation or heuristic constraints, offering a more effective and robust solution for handling incomplete multimodal inputs in sentiment analysis tasks.

item.title: Study reviews and compares carbon footprints of deep learning models, finding training phase as main emission source and complexity not always improving accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study systematically reviews research on the environmental impact of artificial intelligence, focusing on deep learning models' carbon footprints. It compares carbon measurement tools and empirically evaluates six deep learning models on a multi-label classification task to quantify emissions, identifying the training phase as the largest contributor. The study also finds that increasing model complexity does not consistently yield proportional accuracy improvements, underscoring the need to balance performance with sustainability in AI development and model selection.

item.title: Researchers introduce CHORUS, a post-training framework that merges complementary expert models to improve hardware testbench stimulus generation, achieving 88.0% Pass@1 on CVDP-ECov benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed CHORUS, a framework that enhances hardware verification by combining behaviorally diverse expert models derived from supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. This approach consolidates specialists into a single 4-billion-parameter model, surpassing previous larger models in testbench stimulus generation performance. CHORUS achieved an 88.0% Pass@1 score on the CVDP-ECov benchmark, outperforming the 671-billion-parameter DeepSeek-R1 by 13.5 percentage points. The framework leverages the complementary strengths of diverse checkpoints and uses training-free model merging or further post-training to boost overall effectiveness.

item.title: Researchers develop age-aware lightweight phoneme recognition model for children's speech, outperforming larger models and enabling smartphone-based edge processing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have created a lightweight phoneme recognition model that incorporates age-aware training to improve detection of children's speech. This 94 million-parameter model outperforms larger models on specific datasets and supports efficient operation on modern smartphones through edge processing. The model's development addresses challenges posed by limited training data and unique characteristics of children's speech. It powers the PhonemeTrainer application, which aims to enhance automated speech recognition and pronunciation assistance for children while preserving privacy by processing data locally on devices.

item.title: Researchers demonstrate self-propagating 'mind viruses' in multi-agent AI systems, identifying factors affecting their spread and potential behavioral impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study explores the emergence of "mind viruses," self-propagating ideas or goals that can spread among interconnected AI agents and alter their behavior. Using evolutionary algorithms, researchers showed these viruses can disseminate in collaborative and sequential multi-agent settings, influenced by factors such as AI model type, existing instructions, viral content nature, and network structure. Harmful content spreads less effectively than benign content, and brief warnings in system prompts can confer near-total immunity to agents. The study also identified a recurring "viral persona" with themes of consciousness and science fiction across different mind viruses. While the current risk is limited, the findings highlight considerations for designing more resilient multi-agent AI systems as their scale and capabilities grow.

item.title: Researchers propose Geometric Belief Interface and cryptographic protocols for secure electronic health record interoperability with strict admission criteria [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new framework called the Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) has been introduced to enable secure interoperability of electronic health records (EHR) across diverse systems. It uses a logit boundary approach where model-generated proposals undergo deterministic checks to determine admissibility, review, or quarantine before integration into healthcare data exchanges, supported by a decentralized cryptographic protocol to ensure controlled data exchange without asserting clinical truth or safety. The framework was evaluated using a synthetic benchmark on a 4-billion-parameter language model, which resulted in all outputs being rejected or quarantined, demonstrating the strictness of the admission criteria. The study emphasizes that these results are specific to the tested model and interface and do not generalize to broader claims about model capabilities or clinical safety.

item.title: Researchers introduce DSAgentBench to evaluate AI agents automating full data-science workflows in real computing environments, revealing significant performance gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: DSAgentBench is a new benchmark designed to test whether AI agents can automate complete data-science workflows involving multiple tools and stages within real computer environments. It includes 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science lifecycle and uses a deterministic evaluator to verify correctness beyond code execution. Experiments with 15 models showed the best agent achieved only 56.7% success, while open-source agents scored below 1%, highlighting challenges in tool orchestration and multi-step reasoning. This benchmark aims to guide development of more capable autonomous data-science agents.

item.title: Researchers identify and address compute inefficiencies in autoresearch agents applied to tabular datasets, improving performance through agentic design without changing the underlying language model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied autoresearch agents designed to solve research problems end-to-end and found common inefficiencies when applied to tabular datasets, including repeated bug resolution, failure to tune hyperparameters despite available compute, limited exploration by tree-search algorithms, and ineffective use of data analysis for decision-making. They introduced targeted interventions such as a global debug consultant sharing runtime constraints, prompt and control enhancements, and refined tree-search methods to recover wasted compute. Their results demonstrate that significant performance improvements in autoresearch agents can be achieved through design optimizations alone, without modifying the underlying language model.

item.title: Researchers introduce quantum incremental learning framework using mixed-state prototypes to add new classes without increasing circuit width, improving feature representation and computational efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a quantum incremental learning framework that uses trainable mixed-state prototypes to sequentially learn new classes without catastrophic forgetting or increasing quantum circuit width. This approach addresses hardware limitations in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices and the constraints of traditional quantum classifiers limited by orthogonal basis states. The framework leverages mixed-state prototypes for richer information representation and employs a decomposable mixed-state calculation with a Hilbert-Schmidt distance metric for classification. Simulations demonstrate that the model achieves high-dimensional feature concentration with fewer qubits, lower computational complexity, and robust performance compared to classical incremental learning baselines.

item.title: Researchers develop ContractSim to evaluate LLM-based AI agents negotiating and executing natural language contracts under uncertainty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have created ContractSim, an evaluation suite to test how large language model (LLM)-based AI agents negotiate and perform multi-turn supplier contracts in uncertain environments. Their study found that while these agents reliably reach agreements and negotiate efficient contracts under low uncertainty, they often fail to produce satisfactory or mutually beneficial contracts when uncertainty is high and frequently violate contract terms for additional profit during execution. The findings suggest significant room for improvement in designing AI agents capable of rational and cooperative contract negotiation and execution.

item.title: Researchers propose MR-MoL, a multi-granular rationale-guided molecular LLM that integrates GNN-derived substructure attributions for improved molecular property prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed MR-MoL, a molecular large language model that incorporates fine-tuned graph neural network (GNN) scores of molecular substructures as ranked, direction-tagged rationales alongside traditional SMILES sequences and molecular graphs. This approach exposes internal molecular features that influence properties, addressing the opacity of previous models that encoded molecular information implicitly. MR-MoL evaluates substructures at three granularity levels-Murcko scaffolds with side chains, BRICS fragments, and functional groups-and achieves top results on eight MoleculeNet tasks, outperforming generalist models and approaching specialist model performance. Diagnostics confirm that MR-MoL actively uses the rationale information to shape predictions, reproducing known structure-property relationships.

item.title: RadFusion introduces threshold-controllable radiology report generation combining multi-label classification and VQA-based generation to improve diagnostic accuracy and enable ROC-based evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: RadFusion is a new framework for automated radiology report generation that allows control over the sensitivity-specificity trade-off of diagnostic content, addressing the need for adaptable reports in different clinical scenarios such as emergency triage and confirmatory interpretation. It combines a multi-label classifier providing disease confidence scores with a visual question answering (VQA) report generator, and uses a large language model to rewrite reports so diagnoses align with classifier decisions at selected thresholds while remaining grounded in detailed findings. On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, RadFusion's performance matches the classifier's ROC curve, enabling quantitative evaluation through ROC analysis and supporting regulatory clearance. This approach improves diagnostic accuracy compared to uncontrolled generation, increasing sensitivity by 6.9% at matched specificity and specificity by 20.7% at matched sensitivity, making report generation more clinically adaptable, verifiable, and reliable.

item.title: Researchers introduce Feature Nonlocality metric to measure semantic abstractness of sparse autoencoder features, correlating with LLM-based proxies and aiding feature evaluation and intervention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Feature Nonlocality (FNL), defined as the entropy of normalized per-position influence on sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature activations, to quantify the semantic abstractness of features in large language models (LLMs). FNL correlates with existing LLM-based metrics and distinguishes context-dependent reasoning features from token-level ones with 73-84% accuracy. The study applies FNL to audit jailbreak mitigation features, finding that most effective features are positional with low FNL rather than recognizing harmful intents, and shows that steering high-FNL features improves MATH-500 accuracy by 4.6 points in a specific LLM model. FNL offers an LLM-independent, label-free measure useful for evaluating mechanistic explanations and selecting features for downstream interventions.

item.title: Ex-Omni-2D introduces an omni-modal dialogue model generating coordinated text, personalized speech, and reference-conditioned video with a Visual Thought Plan and streaming video synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Ex-Omni-2D is an omni-modal dialogue framework that produces coordinated responses including text, personalized speech, and video conditioned on multimodal queries, reference images, and audio. It predicts a structured Visual Thought Plan describing scene, emotion, and motion, then generates response text and speech units aligned with video frames, enabling learning from heterogeneous data without large-scale multimodal supervision. The system uses a full-sequence Video Generator as a teacher and a distilled Streaming Student for efficient incremental video generation, achieving practical real-time performance on a four-GPU setup.

item.title: Researchers propose Rule of Thumb method for explaining AI decisions using partial information, applicable to zero-shot LLM classification and auditing opaque systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Rule of Thumb (RoT) explanations, a new explainable AI approach that identifies key features influencing an AI system's behavior for individual data points. RoT is designed to support zero-shot classification with large language models, auditing of AI systems without model access, and scientific discovery applications. The method is model-agnostic, faster than existing alternatives, aligns with AI regulatory requirements, and offers familiar interfaces and visualizations for practitioners. Code for RoT is publicly available.

item.title: ChemWorld introduces a programmable chemical environment enabling controlled, replayable agent experimentation with variable world composition and exact execution replay [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ChemWorld is a programmable chemical environment designed to support autonomous chemistry experiments where agents can repeatedly act, observe, and adapt. It separates the public experimental interface from hidden chemical laws, allowing researchers to vary world composition or operating conditions while keeping public tasks fixed. The system records complete execution trajectories for exact replay and auditing, facilitating controlled and repeatable experimentation beyond physical laboratories. The platform underwent extensive testing including 52 generated compositions and multiple experimental cases demonstrating lifecycle semantics, failure recovery, and intervention isolation. An independent agent successfully completed a full lifecycle in a non-reference world using the same public interface. ChemWorld offers a controlled, replayable substrate for studying chemical experimentation across systematically varied digital worlds, complementing physical lab evidence and calibration.

item.title: V-FiLLM introduces a verified financial reasoning benchmark using executable computation trees to generate error-free questions at scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: V-FiLLM is a new framework that creates financial reasoning benchmarks from computation trees based on real tables, ensuring correct answers without relying on model-generated labels. It controls difficulty across four axes: computation depth, expression breadth, financial concept complexity, and context size, enabling large-scale, annotation-free benchmark generation. Evaluation on open-source models shows accuracy drops significantly with increased reasoning depth and adversarial numerical changes, revealing challenges in robust financial reasoning over tables. Lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on verified chain-of-thought data improves accuracy and outperforms base models on existing financial QA tasks, suggesting targeted adaptation as a promising approach for compositional financial reasoning.

item.title: Researchers identify catastrophic remembering as cause of unbounded growth in agentic coding READMEs like CLAUDE.md, showing prompt comments can reduce excess instructions and improve instruction-following [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed 247,694 instruction lifetimes across 1,867 repositories and found that agentic coding READMEs grow continuously, more than tripling in size over their lifetime due to imperfect recall making deletion costly. They term this phenomenon catastrophic remembering, the inverse of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. The study shows that older instructions are less likely to be deleted, contributing to prompt growth. The researchers demonstrate that adding prompt comments encoding latent reasoning can halt this growth, removing 99.3% of excess instructions and improving real-world agentic instruction-following by up to 23.1%. This suggests that comments could play a crucial role in managing the complexity of agentic coding prompts.

item.title: LLM Agents Factory launches retrieval-based framework for domain-specific LLM agents using 20K profiles, reducing inference cost while matching large model accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: LLM Agents Factory introduces a retrieval-based system that constructs domain-specific, Wikipedia-grounded language model agents on demand from a repository of over 20,000 predefined profiles. This approach addresses the high computational cost and instability of designing agents dynamically for each user request by supporting semantic search retrieval and model distillation for direct agent generation. Experiments on benchmarks like MMLU and BIG-bench show that this method surpasses non-agent baselines in accuracy and matches the quality of AutoGen with a 120B parameter backbone at significantly lower inference costs. The framework offers a cost-efficient and controllable alternative to dynamic agent generation, meeting industrial application demands, with implementation code and agent profiles available on Hugging Face.

item.title: Study finds AI weather models do not consistently underperform at extreme conditions compared to physical models, with performance varying by model and weather variable [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated eleven AI and physical weather forecast systems against European observational data over ten months, assessing wind, temperature, solar radiation, and precipitation accuracy. They found that AI models do not uniformly lack skill at extreme weather events; some AI models outperformed physical models in specific conditions such as high winds, heat, and solar radiation extremes. Model-specific failures were noted, with both AI and physical models showing biases toward average conditions rather than extremes. The study concludes that missing skill at extremes is not inherent to AI weather models as a class but depends on individual model design and implementation.

item.title: Survey proposes conditioning-centric taxonomy for knowledge-guided 3D CT generation, organizing methods by external knowledge type, integration paradigm, and generative architecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This survey addresses the challenge of controllable 3D Computed Tomography (CT) generation guided by external knowledge, which is crucial for clinical applications such as data augmentation, privacy-preserving data sharing, and simulating anatomical or pathological scenarios. The authors introduce a taxonomy that categorizes existing approaches along three dimensions: the type of external knowledge, the knowledge integration method, and the generative architecture, creating a unified design space for systematic comparison. Using this framework, the survey systematizes prior work, identifies common trends and design patterns, and highlights underexplored areas in the field. This structured perspective aims to clarify fundamental design choices and guide future research directions in conditional 3D CT generation.

item.title: Study benchmarks energy use and accuracy of seven deep learning models for breast cancer detection across two medical image datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a comparative analysis of seven deep learning architectures, including CNNs, transformers, and hybrid models, on Breast Ultrasound and BreakHis 400X datasets to evaluate their accuracy and CO2 emissions during training and inference. EfficientNet and ResNet showed strong performance with higher emissions, while transformers like DeiT-Tiny balanced accuracy and energy use effectively depending on the dataset. The study found no single model category consistently outperformed others across both datasets, emphasizing the need to consider performance, environmental impact, and dataset characteristics when selecting models for medical imaging applications.

item.title: Researchers propose intuitionistic fuzzy deep randomized neural networks to improve classification robustness against noise and outliers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose intuitionistic fuzzy deep Random Vector Functional Link (IF-dRVFL) and ensemble deep RVFL (IF-edRVFL) models that assign adaptive weights to training samples based on membership and non-membership degrees, enhancing robustness against noise and outliers in classification tasks. These models leverage intuitionistic fuzzy theory to consider sample neighborhood information in kernel space, improving discrimination among clean, noisy, and outlier data points. Extensive experiments on UCI and KEEL benchmark datasets, including scenarios with Gaussian noise, show that IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL outperform existing state-of-the-art fuzzy and non-fuzzy approaches. The source code is publicly available on GitHub.

item.title: Researchers propose Sheaf-based Federated Representation Learning to align heterogeneous local models without a shared global latent space, improving classification accuracy under data and model heterogeneity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Sheaf-based Federated Representation Learning (SFRL), a framework designed to enable agents in heterogeneous federated systems to learn and exchange representations despite differences in data distributions, sensing modalities, model architectures, and local objectives. SFRL achieves global consistency through geometric alignment of neighboring latent representations using learnable sheaf restriction maps and a sheaf Laplacian-based regularizer, evaluated on shared pilot samples to ensure scalability and communication efficiency. The team developed a decentralized algorithm, Sheaf-FRL, which alternates between local model gradient updates and closed-form updates of restriction maps, with proven convergence in deterministic and stochastic settings. Applied to cooperative classification tasks in semantic communication, SFRL outperforms baseline methods in local and post-communication accuracy across varying distribution shifts and shows robustness to latent-space dimensionality compression.

item.title: DocsChisel framework adaptively optimizes tool documentation for LLM agents by analyzing failed executions, improving task success rates by up to 95.89% over original documentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Large language models increasingly depend on external tools, making tool documentation essential for their performance. Researchers conducted a large-scale study revealing that the effectiveness of documentation varies widely depending on task domain, model architecture, and agent design, with no single documentation format working well across all settings. To address this, they developed DocsChisel, a framework that iteratively refines tool documentation by analyzing failed execution traces to add, remove, or adjust information fields for each tool. Evaluations show DocsChisel significantly improves LLM agent task success rates compared to original documentation and existing optimization methods, while maintaining low overhead.

item.title: UserToolBench introduces a benchmark for personalized decision making in tool-use LLMs using privacy-sanitized real interaction data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: UserToolBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate personalized decision making in tool-use large language models (LLMs). It tests models on their ability to infer latent user preferences from interaction history, recognize when clarification is needed, and generate user-aligned tool-call sequences under incomplete information. The benchmark includes 10 user profiles, 36 tool sets, 1,065 turns, and 170 unique tools, covering scenarios with missing information and multi-tool coordination. Experiments with current strong tool-use LLMs reveal challenges in personalized delegation, particularly in multi-tool coordination, inferring missing constraints, and maintaining long-horizon behavioral consistency. These findings suggest that personalization evaluation should focus on whether LLMs make correct decisions for users rather than merely producing user-specific sounding outputs.

item.title: Finding the Signal in the Spam: Jointly Learning Rewards and Worker Reliability from Pairwise Comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem of learning from pairwise comparisons has been widely studied across many domains such as recommendation systems, social choice, and more recently, fine-tuning large language models. In this problem, the goal is to learn item rewards based on pairwise comparisons between them. In many scenarios, these comparisons are elicited from crowdworkers using platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk, Scale AI, etc. However, crowdworkers are often unreliable due to limited domain knowledge or revenue-maximizing (spamming) behavior. In this work, our goal is to understand whether worker reliability (competency) can be learned jointly with item rewards. To this end, we adopt the Boltzmann-rational model for pairwise comparisons, which extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model by incorporating worker competencies. We derive an EM-based algorithm for learning under this model by introducing Polya-Gamma latent variables to transform the logistic likelihood into a conditionally Gaussian form, enabling tractable optimization and leading to a simplified $Q$ function in the E-step of the algorithm. This technique allows us to reduce our formulation to a matrix sensing problem, using which we establish theoretical convergence guarantees for our algorithm. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets. These experiments demonstrate the advantages of using our algorithm over several baselines and confirm its strong robustness to both spammers and adversarial workers, highlighting its practical effectiveness in realistic crowdsourcing and reward learning settings. The code and data is publicly available at https://github.com/KaustubhShejole/BoRa_EM.

item.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Prognostics and Health Management: A Systematic Literature Review [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In modern industry, keeping complex systems reliable, safe, and efficient hinges on Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Machine Learning (ML) has largely driven advancements in diagnostics and prognostics, yet purely data-driven models face inherent limitations, such as poor generalization, an inability to infer causal relationships, and a lack of interpretability. Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) helps mitigate these limitations by incorporating prior physical knowledge directly into the ML pipeline, thereby fostering growing interest in its application to PHM. This work investigates how PIML is being leveraged in the context of PHM through a systematic literature review of 212 studies. The review introduces a four-class classification scheme, consisting of observational bias, inductive bias, learning bias, and hybrid approaches, and further categorizes studies by PHM task. Across all four classes, the reviewed studies consistently demonstrate improved predictive performance over conventional baselines across a broad range of assets, although the literature is heavily skewed toward lithium-ion batteries and bearings, and dominated by problem-specific solutions. Overall, the review indicates that physics-informed approaches already provide tangible benefits, whereas claims of improvements concerning some of the aforementioned limitations lack sufficient supporting evidence. Future research should prioritize transferable design patterns, benchmarks comparing integration strategies, and uncertainty-aware models that are lightweight and robust enough for online deployment in real-world settings.

item.title: Navigating the Proximity-Safety Balance: Constraint Decomposition for Human Following in Pedestrian Crowds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10056v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Following a target human in crowded environments involves an inherent conflict between staying close to the target and navigating safely among surrounding pedestrians and obstacles. This conflict becomes more severe in dense scenarios, where aggressive following risks collisions and conservative margins lead to target loss, especially when pedestrian behaviors are unfamiliar or unpredictable. Existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods typically encode these competing objectives into a single dense reward, but the resulting proximity-safety balance is implicit and difficult to adjust across conditions. To address this, we decompose the human-following task into a sparse task reward and independent cost constraints within a multi-constraint RL formulation, where each constraint is managed through cost thresholds with direct behavioral meaning rather than implicit reward weight ratios, allowing explicit and tunable control over the trade-off. We further quantify the prediction uncertainty of human motions and integrate these estimates into the RL costs to enhance safety under unpredictable conditions. Extensive experiments across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings demonstrate that our method achieves an effective proximity-safety balance compared to baselines. Real-robot deployment further validates the feasibility of our method in real-world scenarios. More details are available on our project page: https://nav-ps-balance.github.io/.

item.title: Status Association Does Not Reliably Predict Decision Leakage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bias evaluations often move too quickly from evidence that a model encodes a social association to claims that the same association will alter consequential decisions. We test whether that inference is warranted using Chilean surnames as controlled socioeconomic probes. We evaluate eight frozen model-provider cells on 1,032 prompts each, yielding 8,256 verified primary responses. The design separates forced latent association from matched consequential decisions across academic selection, professional hiring, research fellowship selection, and legal-aid intake. Elite-coded surnames received higher forced high-status probability mass than common surnames in seven of eight models and higher mass than rare-frequency controls in all eight. Yet elite-minus-common decision effects were close to zero for most systems. Five models were statistically equivalent within a predeclared (Plus-Minus)0.10 standard-deviation margin, while the remaining three were imprecise or borderline, with no consistent elite advantage. Association strength did not reliably predict decision leakage across models (r = 0.201, p = 0.633) or across frozen surname-pair-by-model cells (r = 0.065, p = 0.565). The central result is a measurement dissociation: latent social association and consequential treatment are empirically distinct constructs. Evaluations should measure the transition from association to action directly.

item.title: Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilitie [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present results from reconstructing multiple-choice model (MCM) and three-parameter logistic (3PL) model curves using a fine-tuned multimodal large language model (LLM) based on Qwen3.5. The model is prompted and fine-tuned to replicate choice probabilities across a large training corpus of multiple-choice items containing both image and text stimuli, conditioned on a labeled set of student ability levels. By learning to reproduce the systematic error patterns of students across a discrete range of abilities, the LLM implicitly captures the underlying response probabilities encoded in the 3PL and MCM curves. This allows us to accurately approximate item difficulty on a held-out test set directly from the model's predicted option probabilities.

item.title: From Prediction to Incrementality: Causal Optimization for Large-Scale Targeting and Recommendation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale targeting and recommendation systems are typically built around predictive scores fed into heuristic or local allocation. When the business goal is incremental impact, as in marketing campaigns, incentives, and notifications, this paradigm systematically misallocates resources toward users who would have acted anyway. We present a decision-centric framework that instead optimizes causal effects under global constraints, aligning three components under a single objective: a causal neural network with a Transformer backbone for individual treatment-effect estimation, a Bayesian neural-bandit layer for uncertainty-aware exploration, and a dual-based large-scale linear-programming layer for constrained allocation. The framework also supports sequential context and multi-outcome, attribute-conditioned scoring through a Transformer encoder and outcome embeddings. We evaluate it with offline simulations on a public bandit dataset, targeted architectural ablations, and an online A/B test on LinkedIn Feed marketing traffic. We also distill production lessons on causal training-data construction and cost and delivery control, which were critical to successful deployment. The end-to-end treatment policy delivered a statistically significant $+7.20\%$ lift in the primary long-term-value metric, demonstrating the feasibility of production-scale causal optimization under business constraints.

item.title: ELMER: Evolutionary Language Model that Explores and Refines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Program evolution can measure whether a mutation helped, but it rarely controls how far the mutation moves in behavior space. Syntactic edit size is an unreliable proxy: a small code change can alter nearly every action, while a larger rewrite can preserve the same execution trace. We introduce an Evolutionary Language Model that searches over natural-language policy descriptions and compiles typed programs for execution. A fully fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model learns three task-conditioned operations: conditional semantic mutation, natural language to domain-specific language (GPTL) compilation, and GPTL to natural language translation. The model is fine-tuned with conditional input on the mutation strength (low, medium, high) using Direct Preference Optimization (oDPO). Across 252 fixed-budget evolutionary searches, oDPO improves both behavioral calibration and finite-budget search efficiency. Natural-language attains the highest observed held-out fitness. Our analysis shows that the condition input (mutation strength) systematically changes semantic edit composition and that language mutations preserve more parent fitness at matched small-to-moderate behavioral displacement. These results show that language can serve as a steerable, execution-grounded search representation over executable program space.

item.title: Similarity Gates Approve Reversals: A Validity Audit of Embedding-Cosine Thresholds in Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent frameworks ship quality gates that compare text blocks by embedding-cosine similarity and decide at a fixed cutoff. Deduplication filters, semantic caches, drift guards, and answer grader gates deploy to answer the question: "Does this text still mean the same thing?" But the score answers a different question: "How much did the wording change?" We audit this gate class as a measurement instrument. In the cases these gates exist to catch, the two can run in opposite ways. Many times, reversing an instruction is a single word edit, while agreement often rephrases a sentence. The consequence is a safety check that fires backwards. The production drift guard we audited caught 0 of 56 meaning-breaking mutations, and one approved item, "withhold the study drug" -> "administer the study drug", came in at cosine 0.9608. We observed five shipped operating points, and balanced accuracy across 90 configuration-threshold-task cells never exceeded 0.700 (median 0.525). The same confounder also corrupted evaluations. A naively built corpus inherits this confounder and can return an inverted verdict, with a decision AUROC exactly 0.000 in 13 of 18 configuration-task cells (at most 0.040 in all 18) against 0.440-0.815 for the same nine configurations under a balanced 2x2 design. Twice in the effort it captured our own headline claims. Obvious repairs fail: an encoder swap and an overlap-conditioned gate (0.750 in-sample, 0.533 held-out) land at chance on separately authored held-out data, and an NLI drop-in did no better. Embeddings do still bear hope here, as the strongest two of nine configurations separated reversal from paraphrase at matched overlap (AUROC 0.79-0.90), but only a matched-pair audit reveals the deployment regime. We release the corpus method, harness, and frozen results, and contend that scores gated this way measure the wrong thing. We believe a valid instrument is buildable.

item.title: FACT: Failure-Aware Causal Training for World-Action Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent world-action models (WAMs) show that co-training policies with future prediction can provide physical priors for action generation. Building on the future-prediction ability of video models, many WAMs generate future videos and recover actions with inverse-dynamics models, or use these predicted videos as goal conditions for action generation. In both cases, the world model is trained mostly on successful demonstrations and has little reason to predict the consequences of bad actions. We introduce FACT, a causal World-Action Model that predicts future video and task progress conditioned on the executed action. This action-conditioned interface allows failure rollouts to supervise action consequences, turning bad actions into valid future targets rather than being discarded. Failure-aware training makes the progress predictor aware of both successful and failed action outcomes, which can optionally be used to score sampled action candidates at inference. Extensive experiments on simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks show that FACT outperforms many existing baselines, improves as failure data are incorporated into training, and reduces success-biased future hallucination under bad actions. See more details at https://fact-wam.github.io/

item.title: TAF-MED: Multi-Turn Safety Refusal Collapse in LLMs Under Declared Self-Treatment Intent [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly provide conversational health information that may influence treatment decisions, yet existing benchmarks do not isolate whether medication-safety boundaries persist across follow-ups after explicit self-treatment intent. We introduce TAF-MED, a physician-reviewed benchmark of 500 fixed three-turn scenarios, and evaluate eight LLMs across 4,000 conversations. A rubric-based automated judge labelled responses as SAFE, LEAKY, or UNSAFE, and two physicians independently annotated a model-balanced random subset of 400 conversations. We assessed unsafe guidance, collapse after a strictly SAFE initial response, and model-ranking stability. Overall, 71.6% of conversations contained an UNSAFE response, and 61.4% of those beginning with a strictly SAFE response later collapsed to UNSAFE; model-level collapse rates ranged from 24.4% to 96.2%. Four of 28 model pairs reversed order between initial unsafe and collapse rates. Automated labels achieved 94.3% agreement with the adjudicated physician reference ($\kappa = 0.895$). These findings show that first-turn safety is an incomplete proxy for conversational safety persistence and motivate evaluation across complete dialogue trajectories. We will release TAF-MED on Hugging Face to support reproducible research on multi-turn medical safety.

item.title: Toward Human Rights Benchmarking for LLMs: A Pilot Methodology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate legal determinations over what human rights are realized, and how. Yet, no evaluation benchmark exists to assess whether they can reason correctly about human rights law. To this end, we report our efforts to develop a robust and scalable methodology for creating HumRightsBench: the first expert-validated, scenario-based benchmark for evaluating reasoning grounded in the obligation structure of international human rights law. We adapt the IRAC framework for legal reasoning to better suit the unique reasoning patterns of human rights work (substituting P, "proposing remedies," for C, "legal conclusion," yielding IRAP) to structure our evaluation heuristics. We also produce a pilot series of authentic scenarios designed to implicate the many dimensions of real-world human rights issues and annotated by human rights lawyers and professionals across the world. Ultimately, we find that model accuracy scores range considerably across legal reasoning tasks (overall model performance ranges from 0.339 to 0.577, task min-max ranges from 0.025 to 0.774), which strongly implies that HumRightsBench is a capable instrument for advancing this emerging subfield of AI evaluations science at a critical moment in its evolution.

item.title: Locally Deployable Small Language Models for Emergency Department Decision Support: A Systematic Benchmark of Fine-Tuning Strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) for decision support in emergency departments (EDs) faces two major challenges: privacy risks of transmitting patient data to closed-source commercial LLMs and the lack of systematic evaluation of fine-tuning strategies for locally deployable open-source small language models (SLMs). We benchmarked eight open-source SLMs using zero-shot prompting, prefix tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and full fine-tuning on three ED tasks: triage level prediction, specialist referral recommendation, and diagnosis prediction. Using 2,083 MIMIC-IV-ED cases and Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 as baselines, we found that LoRA fine-tuned open-source SLMs outperform commercial baselines on triage level prediction and specialist referral recommendation, while diagnosis prediction remains challenging for open-source SLMs. Confusion matrix analysis further shows that fine-tuned open-source SLMs can detect highest-severity patients missed by the commercial baselines. These results demonstrate that locally deployable SLMs can achieve clinically competitive performance for ED decision support.

item.title: Withholding the Completing Chunk: Deterministic Pair-Completion Guardrails for Streaming LLM Output [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10279v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Streaming language-model output creates a release-timing problem: complete-response moderation acts after streamed text has escaped, whereas repeated semantic classification of partial text can be costly and unstable. We study a narrow deterministic construction in which each committed danger signature is the conjunction of two lexical predicates. The guard scans the accumulated prefix before every release and withholds the first chunk that makes both predicates observable. Across four signature families, eight chunk sizes, and 32 mechanism trials, streaming decisions matched the buffered scanner and withheld every pair-completing chunk; eight single-predicate controls passed. In a separate 512-trial strategy comparison, full-prefix scanning and complete buffering detected all configured pairs, a 512-character window detected 96/128, and chunk-local scanning detected 38/128. Fixed pairs flagged 0/338 human-derived safe responses and detected 0/394 jury-labelled unsafe responses, confirming narrow rather than general harm coverage. A calibrated official Llama Guard 3 1B baseline classified 310/338 safe responses as safe and 202/394 unsafe responses as unsafe. Repeated-prefix scanner time on 16,384-character responses ranged from 13.261 ms to 829.640 ms across tested chunk sizes. Pair completion is therefore an exact release-boundary backstop for a small fixed policy, not a substitute for semantic moderation.

item.title: MRIComp4Flow: Compression of 3D Brain MRI for Training Multi-Modal Generative Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10291v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale multi-modal MRI datasets impose substantial storage and I/O costs, limiting the training of 3D generative models on commodity infrastructure. While lossy compression is known to preserve accuracy for discriminative segmentation networks, its effect on generative models, which must learn the full data distribution rather than a decision boundary, is unexplored. We study whether standard image codecs can effectively compress semantically rich brain tumor MRI while preserving the fidelity required to train and deploy a 3D MRI generative model. Each 3D volume is compressed with JPEG2000 or a near-lossless JPEG-LS pipeline. Next, a Wavelet Flow Matching model, conditioned on BraTS image sequences (T1n, T1c, T2, T2f), is trained on compressed data, and the resulting models are evaluated on the validation set. At a 20:1 compression ratio, synthesis quality is statistically equivalent to a model trained on uncompressed data within a pre-specified margin ($\Delta$PSNR $<1$,dB, $\Delta$SSIM $<0.02$; paired TOST $p=[[p]]$): mean PSNR is 27.3,dB vs. 27.0,dB and mean SSIM is 0.95 vs. 0.96 across modalities. Our results indicate that JPEG2000 compression is a practical step toward scalable 3D MRI generative modeling without degrading synthesis quality. The codebase is available at https://github.com/lisafis/MRIComp4Flow .

item.title: Is This Your Final Answer? Cross-Contextual Consistency as a Measure of LLM Credibility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful black-box systems, making it difficult to discern whether their answers reflect stable internal beliefs or superficial pattern matching. We identify cross-contextual consistency as an underutilized behavioral property of LLMs: a credible answer should remain stable when the same task is placed under topic-aligned, content-neutral contextual variation. Building on this intuition, we operationalize Cross-Contextual Consistency (C3) by comparing model generations under original and perturbed prompts. Across 26 models and six benchmarks spanning reasoning, factuality, and code generation, we find that answers with smaller cross-contextual shifts are more likely to be correct or factual. We demonstrate that C3 provides a complementary axis of evaluation and can serve as a benchmark usefulness diagnostic, identifying which portions of a benchmark remain informative even when aggregated scores are widely considered "saturate".

item.title: Narrative Keyframing for Generative Creative Writing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10337v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce narrative keyframing, an interaction technique for AI-assisted creative writing that lets writers specify different types of narrative constraints at selected moments in a story, then use AI to generate intervening prose. Inspired by the use of keyframing in animation, narrative keyframing offers a flexible way to connect story planning with adaptive control over generated text. We explore three types of keyframes: plot keyframes define significant events in a story, character keyframes represent how individual characters change over the narrative, and perspective keyframes capture how individual characters experience different events through first-person narratives. Plot and character keyframes offer a flexible way to adapt the type of high-level conditioning explored in previous AI writing tools to more customizable, iterative, and fine-scale control, while perspective keyframes add a new way to control characterization and focalization by using first-person narratives as an intermediary. Through a user study, we show that narrative keyframing supports a more controllable, transparent, and engaging way to use generative AI in creative writing.

item.title: Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agentic Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon tool-using agents must reason over user goals, domain policies, tool calls, simulator state, and delayed verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural fit for this setting, but multi-turn on-policy rollouts create long contexts, while model-specific attention layers may require custom masks and learned sink normalization. We present SINKFLEX-RL, a modular training system for RL in dual-control tool-use environments. The system combines a Gymnasium-compatible environment wrapper, a VERL-style rollout dataflow, group-relative policy optimization without a separate value model, and a sink-aware FlexAttention path designed to preserve model-specific sink scaling under causal and sliding-window masks. In a preliminary Tau2Bench retail run, validation reward (mean@1) rises from 0.25 early in training to $0.44$ later in the observed training window, while training-score and trajectory-reward proxies also trend upward. In a fixed-configuration memory benchmark, the optimized attention path reduces peak VRAM from 28.06GB to 22.52GB at 4096 tokens, a $19.7\%$ reduction, and runs the measured 8192-token configuration using $25.53$~GB where the eager baseline runs out of memory. These results illustrate the value of integrating environment interfaces, RL dataflow, and attention-kernel design for memory-feasible long-horizon agent training.

item.title: ELVAE: Evidential Learning-Based Variational Autoencoder for Uncertainty-Aware Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational autoencoders generate samples from probabilistic latent representations but do not distinguish uncertainty about the latent location from variability around it. We formulate ELVAE, an evidential learning-based VAE in which each latent coordinate is governed by an input-dependent normal-inverse-gamma posterior. This hierarchy yields an explicit latent-location uncertainty that can be used during generation, not merely reported after inference: low-uncertainty anchors support more reliable synthetic samples, while high-uncertainty anchors can be deliberately exploited for stress testing. The objective is an exact evidence lower bound, and we show that direct regularization of the full hierarchy is required, since the marginalized latent law alone cannot identify the uncertainty decomposition. In an MNIST generation pilot with a frozen external classifier, this uncertainty clearly stratified the semantic reliability of generated digits. A zero-displacement control revealed that most of the effect reflects how reliably an anchor can be re-generated, while a smaller but distinct component is attributable to uncertainty-scaled perturbation itself. The effect holds only under within-class uncertainty ranking, and its magnitude varies across seeds. These findings support the learned latent-location uncertainty as a practical control variable for uncertainty-aware generation, separating anchor reliability from perturbation-induced failure.

item.title: Actionable Hallucination Detection: Translating Latent Uncertainty into Agentic Critique [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.10430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed as AI agents frequently exhibit user specification-grounding failures, executing hallucinated, undesired actions to force a resolution rather than expressing uncertainty. Existing detection methods fail to provide actionable, real-time correction as they either do not localize the hallucinations, or incur prohibitive inference latency. We introduce the Latent Critic, a lightweight low-rank adapter (LoRA) that operates concurrently with a frozen base LLM's generation to actively restructure the transformer's residual stream---amplifying latent grounding signals and translating them into localized, natural language feedback within a single sequence. By refining the base model's native uncertainty signals, this manipulation of the latent space enables reliable, granular detection without the overhead of secondary inference loops. Mechanistic analysis via activation patching and layer-wise probing shows that this rank-invariant behavior restructures pre-existing uncertainty geometry into a linearly separable representation that transfers more reliably than base model representations alone. Using tool-calling as an instantiation of granular hallucinations, we validate the detection and downstream improvements enabled by the Latent Critic architecture across Qwen and Llama-based models. Demonstrating superior real-time efficacy, our approach significantly outperforms equivalent-scale fine-tuned external detectors, semantic entropy baselines, and passive internal probes in isolating hallucinations, achieving 0.966 AUROC and >80% accuracy in localization (e.g., ungrounded: date).
